Newborn Wistar rats, specifically neonates of the Albino rat lineage, emerge with a modest body length of 4.26 cm [Lb = 4.26 cm], a value that reflects the altricial developmental strategy typical of murid rodents. This initial size corresponds to a wet weight at birth of 5.82 grams [Wwb = 5.82 grams], placing the pups among the smaller-bodied mammalian neonates relative to adult dimensions. Under standard colony conditions maintained at a thermoneutral temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the gestation period required to produce these altricial young is approximately 22 days [tg = approximately 22 days], a duration consistent with the rapid embryogenesis observed in many small-bodied eutherian mammals. Immediately following parturition, the altricial neonates display limited mobility and depend entirely on maternal care for thermal regulation and nutrition. The suckling juvenile phase is characterized by a marked acceleration in growth, with the nursing offspring gaining mass rapidly as they rely on the dam's milk for their energetic needs. During this pre-weaning period, the pups progress from a state of complete dependence to one of increasing exploratory behavior, preparing them for the nutritional transition that will occur at weaning.

The dietary transition known as weaning marks a critical developmental milestone in the Wistar rat, occurring at 18 days since birth [tx = 18 days since birth] under standard laboratory temperatures of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. At this point, the young achieve nutritional independence from the dam, ceasing to suckle and beginning to consume solid food. The total length at weaning for a typical pup is recorded as 11.321 cm , while the corresponding wet weight at weaning is 47.72 grams [Wwx = 47.72 grams], representing a substantial increase from the neonatal mass. This period of provisioning cessation is followed by the juvenile stage, during which the immature individuals continue to grow and develop without the direct metabolic subsidy of lactation. As the animals progress through the post-weaning period, they gradually approach somatic maturity, though they remain sexually immature for several additional weeks. The growth trajectory during this phase is particularly steep, with both body length and mass increasing steadily as the sub-adult animals prepare for the onset of gonadal maturation and the eventual transition to reproductive adulthood.

Pubertal development in the Wistar rat occurs at distinct times for each sex, with females typically reaching sexual maturity earlier than males. Female pups experience their first vaginal opening, a reliable external indicator of puberty onset, at approximately 37 days since birth [tp = approximately 37 days since birth] when the ambient temperature is held at 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. At this juncture, the wet weight at puberty for females is recorded at around 123 grams [Wwp = around 123 grams], a mass that signifies sufficient somatic growth to support the energetic demands of future reproductive events. In contrast, males undergo preputial separation, the analogous marker of gonadal activation, at a later age of 43.5 days since birth [tp = 43.5 days since birth] under identical thermal conditions. This sexual dimorphism in the timing of reproductive maturation is a common pattern among mammals, often linked to differences in life-history strategies and the relative energetic investment required for male versus female gamete production. The onset of gametogenesis and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis underpin these observable physical changes, marking the transition from an immature juvenile to a reproductively viable adult.

Adult Wistar rats display pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with males attaining a substantially greater ultimate wet weight than their female counterparts. Male individuals reach a maximum adult body mass of approximately 560 grams [Wwi = approximately 560 grams], whereas adult females stabilize at a considerably lower ultimate wet weight of about 330 grams [Wwi = about 330 grams], a difference attributable to divergent selective pressures on body size between the sexes. The naso-anal length of 12-month-old Wistar rats, representing the ultimate body length, has been documented at 27.75 cm [Li = 27.75 cm], providing a standard metric for somatic size in fully mature individuals. Under controlled vivarium conditions maintained at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], healthy breeding females produce litters of approximately 12 pups [N_R_i = litters of approximately 12 pups] and can raise about 7 litters per year [F_R_i = about 7 litters per year], reflecting the species' characteristic high fecundity and rapid generational turnover. This reproductive strategy, combined with a relatively short gestation period, allows the Wistar rat to achieve a high intrinsic rate of population increase under favorable conditions.

The maximum lifespan recorded for female Wistar rats raised under stable laboratory conditions and maintained at a constant temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C] reaches approximately 1400 days [am = approximately 1400 days], equivalent to nearly four years of age. This comparatively extended longevity, unusual among small rodents of similar body mass, is likely influenced by the absence of predation and the controlled, pathogen-free environment typical of modern animal facilities. The period of reproductive senescence in these females typically begins well before the end of their natural lifespan, resulting in a prolonged post-reproductive phase that has been the subject of considerable gerontological research. As individuals approach the completion of their lifespan, they exhibit characteristic signs of physiological decline, including reduced locomotor activity, decreased body condition, and an increased incidence of neoplastic lesions. This progressive deterioration of organ function ultimately culminates in natural mortality, with the oldest documented individuals providing valuable data for understanding the mechanisms of aging in mammalian systems. The Wistar strain thus serves as an important model organism for studying the interplay between body size, reproductive effort, and longevity in a controlled experimental context.
